M13_S01.summary: The sublime (mahaggata) cittas are the 27 cittas that have gone to the vast calm of absorption — 15 of the form sphere and 12 of the formless sphere.
body: A sublime citta (Mahaggata Citta) is so called from 'mahā' (great) and 'gata' (gone to): a citta that has gone over into the vast calm of absorption. It is also called the exalted or lofty consciousness — 'gone' in the sense of having crossed to the further shore.
The sublime cittas are 27 in all, in two classes: the form-sphere cittas (Rūpāvacara), fifteen, and the formless-sphere cittas (Arūpāvacara), twelve.
Rūpa means form or materiality; avacara means moving about, frequenting, resorting to. Rūpāvacara cittas are therefore the cittas that habitually move in and belong to the form sphere.

The form-sphere cittas fall into three groups: form-sphere wholesome cittas (Rūpāvacara Kusala), form-sphere resultant cittas (Rūpāvacara Vipāka) and form-sphere functional cittas (Rūpāvacara Kiriyā).

M13_S02.summary: Five wholesome, five resultant and five functional cittas make fifteen, the five levels within each group being marked off by their jhāna factors.
body: The form-sphere cittas comprise three groups totalling fifteen cittas: five form-sphere wholesome, five form-sphere resultant and five form-sphere functional — each group running through the full five levels of jhāna.
The five levels of jhāna differ from one another by their jhāna factors, that is, by the associated mental factors present: the first, second, third, fourth and fifth jhānas.
First jhāna has five factors: initial application (Vitakka), sustained application (Vicāra), rapture (Pīti), happiness (Sukha) and one-pointedness (Ekaggatā).

Second jhāna drops initial application and keeps sustained application, rapture, happiness and one-pointedness. Third jhāna drops sustained application as well, leaving rapture, happiness and one-pointedness. Fourth jhāna drops rapture, leaving happiness and one-pointedness. Fifth jhāna replaces happiness with equanimity, leaving equanimity and one-pointedness.

The three groups differ only in their ethical nature: the wholesome cittas are the cause, the jhāna kamma being made; the resultant cittas are the result of that jhāna kamma; and the functional cittas create no kamma and yield no result, being the jhāna cittas of an Arahant.

M13_S03.summary: Serenity meditation brings five benefits: a happy abiding here and now, a basis for insight, the higher knowledges, rebirth in the brahmā realms, and the attainment of cessation.
body: The cultivation of serenity meditation brings five benefits.
First, a happy abiding here and now: the mind is at peace, quiet and at ease. Second, it provides the basis for insight meditation, supplying access concentration and absorption concentration.

Third, the higher knowledges and psychic powers: one who reaches the fifth form-sphere jhāna can attain the five mundane higher knowledges — the divine eye, recollection of past lives, the divine ear, psychic power and the knowledge of others' minds.
Fourth, rebirth in the brahmā worlds of the form or formless spheres, according to the level of jhāna attained.

Fifth, the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling: only a Non-returner or an Arahant who has mastered all eight attainments can enter this temporary abiding, which resembles the Nibbāna without residue.

M14_S01.summary: A formless citta is defined by its formless object, by producing rebirth in the formless realms, and by occurring there; its twelve divide into wholesome, resultant and functional.
body: A formless citta (Arūpa) is so called in three senses: first, it takes a formless meditation subject as its object, something that is not materiality; second, it yields the result of rebirth in a formless jhāna realm; third, any citta that occurs in the formless sphere is called a formless citta.
In the formless realms there is no materiality at all, only mind: no shape, no visible form, no material phenomena of any kind.
The formless-sphere cittas form three groups: four wholesome formless-sphere cittas, four resultant and four functional — twelve cittas in all.

The resultant formless cittas perform three functions: rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death. One who develops, for instance, the wholesome citta of the base of infinite space takes rebirth by the resultant citta of that same base, is sustained by it as life-continuum throughout the life, and dies with it.

M14_S02.summary: Infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness and neither-perception-nor-non-perception differ not by jhāna factors but by the object on which the mind is gathered.
body: First, the base of infinite space (Ākāsānañcāyatana): ākāsa is space, ānañca is boundlessness, āyatana is base or abode — the abode of boundless space. To reach it one must see the danger in materiality and wish to be free of it: entering the fifth form-sphere jhāna by means of one of the nine kasiṇas (excluding the space kasiṇa), emerging, removing the kasiṇa sign and attending to 'infinite space' until absorption arises.

Second, the base of infinite consciousness (Viññāṇañcāyatana): the abode of boundless consciousness. Seeing that the base of infinite space is still unstable and liable to fall back towards the form jhānas, one takes the citta of infinite space itself as object and attends to 'infinite consciousness'.

Third, the base of nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana): one takes as object the absence, the having-passed-away, of the base of infinite space or infinite consciousness, and attends to 'there is nothing at all'.

Fourth, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (Nevasaññā-nāsaññāyatana): one takes the base of nothingness as object. Here consciousness is so subtle that it can be called neither perception nor the absence of perception.

All formless jhānas have the same two factors, equanimity and one-pointedness, becoming subtler at each level. The four differ by the object on which the mind is gathered — each surpassing the base below it — not by the elimination of jhāna factors as in the form sphere.

M14_S03.summary: Four wholesome, four resultant and four functional formless cittas make twelve; the functional ones are the formless jhānas of an Arahant.
body: The formless-sphere cittas form three groups totalling twelve: four wholesome formless cittas (infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, neither-perception-nor-non-perception), four resultant cittas corresponding to those four, and four functional cittas.
The resultant formless cittas are brought about by the wholesome formless cittas: the wholesome citta is the cause and the resultant citta its fruit.
The functional formless cittas belong to Arahants who attain these formless absorptions; creating no kamma, they bear no result.
The plane of rebirth corresponds to the attainment: whichever formless base one develops with wholesome consciousness, into that very formless realm one takes rebirth.

M7_S01.summary: A supramundane citta is a conditioned consciousness that takes the unconditioned — Nibbāna — as its object; there are four paths and four fruitions.
body: Lokuttara citta — supramundane consciousness — is the consciousness that knows an object beyond the world.

Its distinguishing feature is this: it is itself a conditioned state, yet it takes the unconditioned as its object. Conditioned states arise and pass away; the unconditioned is the deathless, unborn state — Nibbāna.
Counted in the extended way the supramundane cittas number 40; counted by their two basic classes there are four path cittas and four fruition cittas.
The two classes are: A. Lokuttara Magga Cittāni, the supramundane path cittas, four in number; and B. Lokuttara Phala Cittāni, the supramundane fruition cittas, also four.

M7_S02.summary: The four paths — stream-entry, once-return, non-return and Arahantship — are each immediately followed by their fruition, and each path citta arises with the whole Noble Eightfold Path.
body: The path cittas are: 1. Sotāpattimaggacittaṃ, the path of stream-entry, the first path; 2. Sakadāgāmimaggacittaṃ, the path of once-returning, the second; 3. Anāgāmimaggacittaṃ, the path of non-returning, the third; 4. Arahattamaggacittaṃ, the path of Arahantship, the fourth.

The fruition cittas are: 1. Sotāpattiphalacittaṃ, the fruit of stream-entry; 2. Sakadāgāmiphalacittaṃ, the fruit of once-returning; 3. Anāgāmiphalacittaṃ, the fruit of non-returning; 4. Arahattaphalacittaṃ, the fruit of Arahantship.
'Sotāpattimagga' is analysed thus: sota is the stream, āpatti is entering into, magga is the path — the consciousness that steps into the stream of the noble path.

Every path citta arises together with the eight path factors, that is, the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration — all eight arising simultaneously in that one mind-moment.

M7_S03.summary: The path of stream-entry destroys personality view, doubt and clinging to rites, realises Nibbāna for the first time, and closes the door to the lower realms.
body: The first path citta arises with the eight path factors; with it one enters the stream of the noble path for the first time.

It destroys three defilements: personality view (taking the body-mind to be a self), doubt (uncertainty about the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha), and clinging to rites and rituals (the belief that ceremonies, superstitions and mere observances bring liberation).
Wisdom is the leading force here, tearing apart the veil of ignorance. This is the first realisation of Nibbāna.
The result: one who has attained the first path can never again fall into the planes of misery.

Four causes bring a path citta into being: (1) meeting a true person — one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma and the canonical texts, not according to private opinion; (2) hearing the true Dhamma; (3) wise attention — attention directed towards Nibbāna and conducive to liberation; (4) practising in accordance with the Dhamma all the way to path and fruit, that is, practising the four foundations of mindfulness, insight meditation rather than serenity alone.
Note that the first path citta does not arise in the formless realms, since the four causes cannot be met there: there is no bodily form, and so no hearing of the Dhamma.
